title: Building a budget
objective: Build a 50/30/20 budget and a zero-based budget from the same payslip

sources.name: ASIC Moneysmart: How to do a budget

q.prompt: A popular budgeting rule splits take-home pay three ways. Guess: what share goes to **savings and extra debt repayments**?
q.explanation: The 50/30/20 rule puts 20% towards savings and paying debt down faster, 50% to needs and 30% to wants.

options.text: A plan for where your money goes, made before you spend it
A record of what you already spent
options.why: That's tracking. A budget is the plan you track against.

options.text: A way to cut out everything fun
options.why: A good budget plans for fun too, so you can enjoy it guilt-free.

q.explanation: A budget is a plan made in advance. Tracking (next lesson) shows how reality compares to the plan.

screens.title: Method 1: the 50/30/20 split
screens.body: Start from [[take-home pay]], not salary. Then aim for about **50%** on needs, **30%** on wants and **20%** on savings and extra debt repayments. It's a starting point, not a law: in a pricey rental market, needs often run higher.

screens.title: Method 2: zero-based
screens.body: Give **every dollar a job** before the month starts. Income minus everything you plan to spend, save and repay should equal **$0**. Savings isn't 'what's left over'; it's a line in the plan, like rent.

screens.title: Paid weekly or fortnightly?
screens.body: Budgets are monthly, but pay often isn't. Multiply weekly pay by 52, or fortnightly pay by 26, then divide by 12. Don't use ×4 or ×2: a year has 52 weeks, so some months hold an extra payday.

screens.title: Worked example: Lena, a nurse
screens.body: Lena is a nurse earning $60,000 a year, paid monthly. Tax comes out before her pay lands. Her employer's {{sgRate}} [[super]] goes to her fund on top, not into her bank.

screens.title: Lena's 50/30/20
screens.body: She rounds take-home pay to **$4,200** to keep it simple.

q.prompt: Tap the line that belongs to Lena but **never reaches her bank account**.
q.hint: Tax goes to the ATO, not to her. Which line is still her money?
q.explanation: Super is Lena's money, paid into her super fund for retirement, so it's not part of her budget today.

q.prompt: Using $4,200 take-home pay, how much does the 50/30/20 rule give Lena for **wants**?
Match each item to its 50/30/20 bucket.
q.hint: Needs keep you housed and fed; savings build your future.
q.explanation: Rent is a need, a concert is a want, and building an emergency fund counts as savings.

q.prompt: Jake takes home $420 a week from his casual shifts. What is that per month, to budget with?
q.explanation: $420 × 52 = $21,840 a year, and ÷ 12 = $1,820 a month. Using ×4 would give $1,680 and miss an extra payday.

q.prompt: Lena's zero-based plan for $4,200: rent $1,550, groceries $520, transport $210, bills $240, fun $700 and savings $600. How much still needs a job?
q.explanation: She's planned $3,820, so $380 still needs a job, like extra savings or paying debt.

q.prompt: Omar is paid fortnightly and takes home $2,600. Under 50/30/20, how much should he aim to save each fortnight?
q.explanation: 20% of $2,600 = $520 a fortnight. The rule works for any pay cycle.

q.prompt: Put the steps for building a budget in order.
q.explanation: Start from what actually lands, cover needs, pay yourself first, then plan wants, and adjust as you learn.

screens.title: Try it on your pay
screens.body: Find your take-home pay for one pay period: a payslip, your banking app, or just your pocket money. Paid weekly? × 52 ÷ 12 for a month. Shifts vary? Use a quieter pay.

bullets: Budget from take-home pay, not salary.
50/30/20: needs, wants, then savings and extra debt.
Zero-based: give every dollar a job until $0 is left.

reviewBank.prompt: Take-home pay is $3,500 a month. Under 50/30/20, how much is for **needs**?
Income $3,000. Planned: rent $1,200, food $450, bills $300, fun $400, savings $500. How much is still unassigned?
You should build your budget from your salary before tax.
reviewBank.explanation: Budget from take-home pay: the amount that actually lands in your account after tax.
